answer_json.answer: No more than 20,000 shares

lesson_text: No more than 20,000 shares. Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 2 million is 20,000. Owning more makes your own selling push the price against you. The stop sets one limit, here 60,000 shares, and the volume rule sets another. The size is the smaller. Splitting the buy into pieces does not change what you own. Size is the smaller of what the stop allows and what the stock's volume can carry.

lesson_text: Move the stop to breakeven. Our rule puts that move between 2R and 5R, ideally, and 2.37R is inside it. lesson_text: Yes, you may hold. The rule lets a trade ride through a report only if it is up 5R. Risk per share is 50.00 minus 48.00. The gain is 61.20 minus 50.00, more than five times that risk. That much cushion means a gap against you leaves much of the gain. A smaller gain has too little cushion, and a stop cannot catch an overnight gap. Above the IPO AVWAP, the average buyer since listing is in profit.

The launch only counts after that pinch. A launchpad is a long rest under averages that pinched together, then the day price clears them.

lesson_text: A short rest after a near-double. A quiet, liquid stock nearly doubles in weeks, then pauses a little under its high. The pause is a rest, not a sale. A high tight flag is a rocket catching its breath for a few weeks, a little under the high.

answer_json.answer: Sell at the stop, as planned

lesson_text: Sell at the stop. After the entry, the stop is the exit, with the time stop and the trail. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. You sized the trade from that stop, so the loss is the one you planned. SRRK, December 2020, had the biggest pole in our research, 291% in 34 sessions. But the breakout day traded about a tenth of its average volume. It was stopped the next session. Quiet breakout volume can lower the grade, our judgment of how clean the setup is. It is not a reason to exit. The stop is an appointment, not a debate. Even after a perfect-looking pole.

lesson_text: Sell a big part into it. For a climax run on your own long, our rule is to sell a big part into it. That is a judgment call. These breakouts often go vertical. lesson_text: The 200-day simple average. We take no longs below it, unless it is a parabolic long. Under the 200-day there is no pullback to buy, only a bounce.

answer_json.answer: The first retest after the pop

lesson_text: The first retest of the averages after the pop. Early in a new up-leg the doubters sell the first pullback. If the averages hold anyway, the selling had no follow-through, and buyers can step in. That is why this first test is the one we trade. One close back over the 20 EMA is only a pop setting up. The crossback is the first pullback to the averages after the pop, where early doubters sell and buyers can step in.

A cross of the 9 under the 20 EMA

answer_json.answer: Keep the stop; buy fewer shares

lesson_text: Keep the honest stop and buy fewer shares. The stop comes first, and the size comes from it: shares equal the account times the risk percent, divided by entry minus stop. A wider stop means fewer shares for the same risk, so the loss stays what we planned. A stop of 3.4% is inside what we accept: 1 to 3% preferred, 3.5% good, up to 5% acceptable. A wide stop can also mean a violent pullback, a warning in itself. A wider stop means fewer shares, never a tighter stop to keep the same size.

answer_json.answer: The averages sit right under price

lesson_text: The averages sit right under price at a crossback, so the low that gives the stop is close to the buy. Kell says that when he buys off support it is usually against the 10 or 20 EMA, and he uses that low as his stop. A close stop means the same risk buys more shares. If the low breaks, the idea is wrong, so little is lost finding out. A crossback stop is close because the averages sit right under price.

Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best. A short is a long setup reversed, so the same holds. The short on this chart, EXP, was up 3R by day 3 and did not stop there. Rarely cover on day 1. Day 3 at the earliest, often into a longer move.

At exactly 3R, whatever the day
Day 1, to lock in a quick gain
Never; hold it all to the end

answer_json.answer: Cut longs; the market is weak

lesson_text: Cut long exposure. The index's own Wedge Drop is a reason to cut exposure in any market. It is a warning that the market as a whole is weakening. Kell: ideally any long positions have been closed at the Wedge Drop. Bracco called the Nasdaq's drop the start of another leg down. On this chart the index was back over both averages within a week, so the warning was short. The rule is about cutting exposure, not about calling the next leg. When the index wedge drops, your longs are on notice. Reduce first, ask later.

answer_json.answer: Long, when the breakdown fails

lesson_text: Long, when the breakdown fails. The breakdown everyone sees never comes, or comes and fails, and the squeeze fuels the next leg up. Bracco: the only way to trade a head and shoulders is to trade its failure. We never short the right shoulder before the neckline breaks, and a break is not taught here as a short setup. A fall of more than 10% under the neckline means the top worked, and the setup is gone. ABNB in June 2026 drew this top, fell 3.0% under the neckline, and recovered. The buy over the right shoulder reached 3R in 9 days. The top everyone sees is the trade when it fails. We buy the failure.

Long, when the breakdown fails

answer_json.answer: A neckline break, bought back

lesson_text: A neckline break that is bought back. Version B on our card is at least one close under the neckline, or an intraday undercut of the right armpit low, that does not fall more than 10% under the neckline before the trigger. Murphy: once the neckline has broken, any decisive close back above it is a serious warning that the breakdown was probably a bad signal. Version A is the card's lesser form, with no close under the neckline at all. NFLX in April 2025 fits: it fell 6.0% under the neckline and failed within two weeks, and the buy over the right-shoulder high reached 3R in 3 days. Version B is a real break that failed. The crowd sold the break; the stock refused.

A small gap over the level is the trigger, filled at the open. A big one is a chase.

answer_json.answer: An Oops reversal day

lesson_text: An Oops. It opens under the prior close, trades under the prior day's low and reclaims the prior close the same day. A Holy Grail's trigger comes after a touch of the 20 EMA, and this stock never touched it. A U&R undercuts a level everyone can see, such as a bounced swing low or the range low. A Slingshot needs 3 to 7 closes under the 4-day EMA of the highs, then a close back over it. Nothing here shows that. Read the trigger. One day's open-and-reclaim is the Oops; a touch and a push over the high is the Grail.

choices: An Oops reversal day
A Holy Grail
A swing-low U&R
A Slingshot

Buy again only on a new trigger.

answer_json.answer: Do not fade it; let it run

lesson_text: Do not fade it. Breitstein's marks of a steady drive: the slope is consistent, about a 1:1 angle upward, and candle size contracts over time. Of such a drive he wrote that there was no logical short setup, and losses from fighting this trend were entirely avoidable. Our card lists fading a steady drive as a mistake. And we short only below the 200-day, so this drive is no short for us. A steady drive is a trend to respect. Fading it is the avoidable loss.
